summary:
We developed a concept for a safe, science-driven lunar landing mission at the Moon’s south pole. Our proposed landing site is Connecting Ridge, between Shackleton and de Gerlache craters, because it offers relatively open terrain, strong solar exposure, and a practical line of sight for Earth communications, while remaining close to permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) that may contain water ice.

The mission uses a lander and a small rover. The lander performs a precision landing on a stable, sunlit area, then deploys the rover to explore nearby PSRs and search for water ice and other volatile resources. To solve the south pole’s communication challenge, we use a hybrid system: direct-to-Earth communication when Earth is visible, plus lunar relay satellites for continuous coverage. The rover communicates with the lander through a local surface network, and the lander stores important data during communication gaps.

This approach addresses the challenge by balancing landing safety, power availability, communications reliability, and scientific value. It is important because confirming and using lunar water ice could support future human exploration, fuel production, and a sustainable presence on the Moon.
details:
Project Details

Our project is a mission concept for a safe and scientifically valuable landing at the lunar south pole. We selected Connecting Ridge, between Shackleton and de Gerlache craters, as our primary landing site because it combines relatively open terrain, good solar exposure, a practical communication link to Earth, and proximity to permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) that may contain water ice.

How it works

The mission consists of a lander and a small rover.

  • The lander performs a precision landing on a stable, sunlit area of Connecting Ridge.
  • It uses solar panels and rechargeable batteries to operate during periods of low sunlight.
  • The lander carries communication equipment, scientific instruments, and a rover deployment system.
  • The rover travels to nearby permanently shadowed regions to analyze the surface and search for water ice and other volatile materials.
  • The lander acts as the main communication and data-relay station for the rover.

Communication solution

Communications at the lunar south pole are difficult because Earth is not always visible from the surface. Our design uses a hybrid communication system:

  • Direct-to-Earth communication when Earth is within line of sight.
  • Lunar relay satellites to maintain contact when Earth is not visible.
  • A local surface network between the lander and rover.
  • A store-and-forward data system, which saves scientific data and telemetry during communication interruptions and transmits it later.

This makes the mission more reliable and reduces the risk of losing valuable data.

Benefits and impact

Our project supports future lunar exploration by identifying a landing location that is both safe and scientifically valuable. Confirming water ice near the lunar south pole could help future missions produce drinking water, oxygen, and rocket propellant on the Moon. This would reduce the amount of supplies that must be launched from Earth and support a long-term human presence on the lunar surface.

The mission also improves our understanding of the Moon’s history, surface conditions, and available resources.

Tools and development

Our team developed the project through research, mission planning, and design work. We used:

  • NASA and scientific sources to study lunar south pole landing sites, illumination, communications, and water ice.
  • Lunar maps and crater data to compare possible landing locations.
  • Diagrams and slides to present the mission architecture, rover path, communication system, and landing-site selection.
  • Engineering-design thinking to consider power, temperature, terrain safety, communication coverage, and scientific objectives.

Creativity

The creative part of our project is the combination of a practical landing site with a complete surface-exploration and communication plan. Instead of choosing only a famous crater, we selected a location that balances safety, sunlight, communication, and access to scientifically important shadowed regions.

We also designed a mission that does not rely on one communication method. By combining direct-to-Earth communication, relay satellites, and local rover communication, our system can continue operating even when conditions at the lunar south pole are difficult.

Factors we considered

Our team considered several important factors:

  • Safe and relatively flat landing terrain.
  • Availability of sunlight for solar power.
  • Distance from permanently shadowed regions.
  • Risk of contaminating scientifically valuable ice deposits with engine exhaust.
  • Reliable communication with Earth.
  • Rover mobility and power requirements.
  • Protection of electronics from extreme cold.
  • The scientific value of searching for water ice.

Overall, our project presents a realistic and well-balanced approach to landing, exploring, and communicating at the Moon’s south pole.
